Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivered remarks Wednesday afternoon after the central bank opted to raise interest rates by 0.25 percent to tame inflation amid the Iran war.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to increase the rate to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent, its first hike in over three years — and the first time in nearly a year the figure touched 4 percent.

The bank has faced growing pressure from President Trump to slash rates, and the latest decision risks throwing a wrench into Warsh’s relationship with the president.

articles.title: Tax breaks helping fuel Trump's latest tech push just landed in Dems' crosshairs
articles.summary: House Democrats target bonus depreciation and opportunity zone tax breaks for AI data centers, arguing Big Tech shouldn't get taxpayer subsidies.
articles.body: House Democrats are moving to stop data centers from receiving lucrative federal tax breaks as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom accelerates their expansion nationwide. The moves put Democrats at odds with President Donald Trump as he makes data centers central to his American AI agenda. The administration has sought to accelerate data center development and streamline permitting as the U.S. competes for dominance in the emerging tech industry. Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., and Don Davis, D-N.C., unveiled legislation Wednesday that would block data centers from tapping certain federal investment incentives. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY The incentives in question weren't created specifically for AI or data centers. But the industry's massive infrastructure investments can qualify for these substantial tax benefits, which prompted Democrats to push to exclude data centers as concerns grow over electricity demand, water use and local development. The bill is backed by 21 additional House Democrats, including Ways and Means Committee member Rep. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif. "Washington is giving handouts to Big Tech companies while American families are drowning. I hear that word in my district more than any other," McDonald Rivet said at a news conference Wednesday. "From rising costs, groceries, gas, housing, healthcare and a lot more. These are backward priorities, and they perfectly encapsulate everything that is wrong with the way Washington works, serving interests of big corporations and special interests at the expense of working people." THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS Speaking alongside McDonald Rivet outside the Capitol, Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., pointed to concerns over data center development in her Raleigh-area district, accusing tech companies of buying land without disclosing their plans in a plot to sidestep local input. "They've sought to bypass local citizens' right to provide input on putting a data center in their towns and cities," Ross said. The lawmaker also argued that the industry's rapid expansion is straining electricity and water resources while developers benefit from federal and state tax incentives. "It's Americans struggling to get by, not Big Tech who need tax breaks," Ross said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., argued that data center development is contributing to higher costs for his constituents as the facilities place growing demands on electricity and water supplies. He also said communities should have more control over where the facilities are built. "Our cities and towns shouldn't have these data centers shoved down their throats without any recourse," Pappas said. "They deserve the right to decide what's appropriate for their community."

articles.title: ‘Rickroll’ and ‘looksmaxxing’ are official: Merriam-Webster adds 1,400 new words to dictionary website
articles.summary: Merriam-Webster.com has added 1,400 new words and definitions to its dictionary, including looksmaxxing, parasocial, and rickroll.
articles.body:
( WWLP ) – Merriam-Webster.com has added 1,400 new words and definitions to its dictionary, reflecting the widespread use of updated and evolving language.

Among the new entries are words stemming from social media . It’s not surprising, given the internet’s impact on how people speak with and understand one another. They include:

Looksmaxxing: the practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness

Parasocial : relating to or involving a one-sided emotional connection with someone (especially a celebrity or fictional character) whom one does not know personally

Rickroll : to trick (someone) into hearing the song “Never Gonna Give You Up” by English singer Rick Astley

As technology evolves, new definitions in that arena enter the general lexicon, such as the word compute as a noun, defined as “the computational resources (such as memory and processing power) required for a computer or computer program to function.”

Additional entries include AGI (artificial general intelligence), vibe coding (using AI to create computer code) and uncanny valley (an uneasy feeling you get in response to human simulation).

In the food category, Merriam-Webster expanded its palette with items such as cake pop , shishito, bao and chili crisp . The term superfood, defined as “a food (such as salmon, broccoli, or blueberries) that is rich in nutrients,” also made its debut.

Modern terms that have appeared in recent years have also received official definitions, shaped by pop culture and shared experiences. Examples include:

Cuffing season: a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with

Yacht rock: a style of soft rock music originating in the 1970s and 1980s

Crashout : A: a mental or emotional breakdown, B: an emotional outburst or tantrum

Sunday scaries : feelings of anxiety or sadness that arise on Sunday from the knowledge that the weekend is almost over

Copium: avoidance, denial, or minimization (as of a bad situation, problem, outcome, etc.) imagined as a narcotic

Mandela Effect : the experience of many people having the same false memory (coined by researcher Fiona Broome , who remembered the prison death of former South African President Nelson Mandela, though that didn’t happen.)

For a full list of the new entries, visit Merriam-Webster.com . It is the oldest dictionary company in the United States and is headquartered in Springfield, Mass.

articles.title: House votes to hold Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
articles.summary: The House of Representatives voted unanimously Wednesday to find billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for refusing to comply with subpoenas related to a congressional probe into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
articles.body: The House of Representatives voted unanimously Wednesday to find billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for refusing to comply with subpoenas related to a congressional probe into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Members passed the measure by unanimous consent one day after the House Oversight Committee voted 41-0 recommending the full House take action against Black for refusing to fully cooperate with its investigation into Epstein. The resolution says “Mr. Black’s willful refusal to comply with the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas constitutes contempt of Congress and warrants referral to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia for prosecution as prescribed by law.” Attorneys for Black, co-founder and former head of the prestigious investment firm Apollo Global Management, released a statement calling the House measure an “outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black.” “The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee’s actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer,” they wrote. Earlier this month, Black sued the Oversight Committee, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued for his appearance and nondisclosure agreements tied to Epstein. Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the committee chair, said Wednesday’s action shows that “No one is above the law. Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the U.S. House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress.” The top Democrat on the panel, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, called the vote “an important step towards justice and accountability.” He said members need to know why Black “gave Jeffrey Epstein $180 million dollars.” Black had a lengthy business relationship with Epstein, a financier who died in jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. Black announced he was stepping down as Apollo CEO in January 2021 after an internal review found he had paid Epstein $158 million between 2012 and 2017 for advice on tax and estate planning services. The review found that Black was not involved in Epstein’s criminal activities. Black has said he didn’t engage in any wrongdoing and “deeply” regrets his involvement with Epstein, who died in jail in 2019 awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. Black hasn’t been accused of wrongdoing by law enforcement, and he has denied any involvement in or awareness of Epstein’s illegal activity. Black voluntarily sat for a closed-door transcribed interview with the Republican-led committee in late June, but it ended early with lawmakers slapping him with two subpoenas for allegedly not being forthcoming. Attorneys for Black said the questioning went well beyond the parameters of the panel’s investigation and accused the lawmakers of engaging in a fishing expedition. “This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black,” one of the lawyers, Susan Estrich, said earlier this month. He didn’t show up for a deposition the committee scheduled for Sept. 3 and filed suit against the panel. In a statement Tuesday, Black’s attorneys called the contempt action “retaliation” for their client exercising his constitutional rights.

articles.title: Colbert tells Kimmel he doesn’t miss late night, compares news to ‘a cup of poison every day’
articles.summary: Comedian Stephen Colbert on Tuesday told late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that he does not miss hosting CBS’s “The Late Show” and compared talking about the news to taking “a cup of poison every day.” A bearded Colbert, resembling his late-night predecessor David Letterman after he departed “The Late Show” in 2015, appeared as a guest…
articles.body:
Comedian Stephen Colbert on Tuesday told late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that he does not miss hosting CBS’s “The Late Show” and compared talking about the news to taking “a cup of poison every day.”

A bearded Colbert, resembling his late-night predecessor David Letterman after he departed “The Late Show” in 2015, appeared as a guest on ABC’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” The eponymous host told Colbert he looked happier and healthier, adding that he seemed “like a different person.”

“Like I don’t drink a cup of poison every day?” Colbert replied. “Because part of the job is of –– the old gig, as I remember it, was to be lowered like carbon rods into a radioactive pool every day and then to be pulled out and put in front of a camera and to irradiate it back at the audience at a non-lethal rad level.”

Kimmel quipped that was “exactly the job description.” He then referred to a picture they took at the Primetime Emmy Awards on Monday with fellow late-night hosts Jon Stewart and John Oliver, adding that the photographer joked they were all at “the endangered table.”

“And if you can see, I’m smiling, but I literally said this under my breath, ‘That joke’s not as funny as you think,'” Colbert said, prompting laughs from Kimmel’s audience.

Separately, Colbert told CNN’s Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety’s Ramin Setoodeh after the Emmy Awards that free speech was “alive and well,” but that late-night remains an important part of television despite criticism, Variety reported .

“Because if you can’t say something because you go to jail, that is a violation of free speech,” Colbert said. “I think that late night is just as funny and just as vital as it ever has been, and I love watching Jimmy [Kimmel] and Jimmy [Fallon] and John [Stewart] and Jon [Oliver] and Seth [Meyers] and everybody else.”

“And I think I hope it goes on for a long time because you get to work with people like this, and that’s the greatest gift,” he added.

Colbert stepped down from his role earlier this year after CBS’s parent company, Paramount, announced the show’s cancellation in 2025. He read the day’s headlines as part of his opening monologue but cracked light-hearted jokes that avoided partisan politics or references to President Trump, one of Colbert’s most frequent targets.

Paramount Skydance is owned by Larry and David Ellison, a father-son duo allied with the president.

Trump and other conservatives frequently attack the late-night hosts over their criticisms and jokes. The president at times has called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to investigate Kimmel for allegedly violating “equal time” restrictions for political candidates, including a recently pulled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D).

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, an appointee of former President Biden, last week said that the decision not to broadcast the interview after Trump’s latest threat was one of the administration’s attempts to stifle free speech.

articles.title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
articles.summary: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.
articles.body:
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis.

In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.

Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.

In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda".

Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.

In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer.

"Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."

Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.

Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.

In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.

Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.

In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.

For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."

She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."

The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.

President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

articles.title: Russian spies orchestrated $40K murder plot in nation’s capital, US alleges
articles.summary: Five Russian intelligence operatives allegedly offered $40,000 to a U.S.-based recruit to kill a Kremlin critic believed to live in Washington, D.C.
articles.body: The U.S. accused Russian intelligence operatives of orchestrating a murder-for-hire plot targeting a Kremlin critic believed to be living in Washington, D.C. In documents unsealed on Tuesday, federal prosecutors claim the conspiracy was part of a broader global network that recruited people to carry out assassinations and terrorist attacks on behalf of Moscow. The five men charged in the incitement allegedly worked for Russia's intelligence services, and are accused of being paid and attempting to pay others in the U.S. and abroad to surveil and kill Russian dissidents. Three of the defendants also face conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire charges. All five defendants remain at large, according to the Justice Department. According to prosecutors, the alleged operation reached the nation's capital in late August, when suspected Russian intelligence operatives directed a U.S.-based Venezuelan citizen to secretly film two Washington-area locations tied to a Kremlin critic before allegedly offering him $40,000 to carry out the killing. The recruit completed the surveillance but refused to commit the murder himself, according to the indictment. Prosecutors allege the five defendants were members or associates of a Russian intelligence-directed network that financed terrorism and coordinated violent operations across multiple countries. The recruiter walked the operative through the surveillance step by step, prosecutors say, and allegedly instructed him to put his phone in airplane mode, begin recording before entering the neighborhood, slow as he passed the target's home and delete the messages afterward. The indictment says the conspirators used coded language, referring to the assassination as "construction" and the surveillance as "measuring a plot of land." When the recruit declined to carry out the murder himself, prosecutors allege the network sought other U.S.-based recruits while noting it also had "people in Mexico" available for the job. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT In addition to the alleged murder plot in Washington, the indictment accuses members of the network of supporting attacks on civilian and military infrastructure in Europe and carrying out surveillance of Russian dissidents abroad. The case marks one of the most serious publicly alleged Russian intelligence operations targeting an individual inside the U.S. in recent years. The indictment names five alleged members of what prosecutors call the Russian Intelligence Services Network (RIS). They are Yuri Khrameev, a former Russian intelligence colonel known as "Colonel Yuri"; his son, Kirill Khrameev, an officer in Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB); Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban national living in Russia whom prosecutors describe as coordinating attacks for the network; Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as "Viking," and Angel Eduardo Castro. Russia has repeatedly been accused by Western governments of targeting political opponents and defectors abroad. Among the highest-profile cases was the 2018 poisoning of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury, England, with the military-grade nerve agent Novichok. British authorities blamed Russian military intelligence for the attack, an allegation Moscow denied. U.S. officials have also accused Russia of orchestrating killings of Kremlin critics overseas and conducting covert influence and espionage operations inside the United States, though prosecutors say the alleged Washington murder plot represents a rare instance in which Russian operatives sought to recruit someone on U.S. soil to carry out an assassination. RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY Prosecutors say the alleged Washington murder plot was part of a much broader Russian intelligence campaign that has operated since at least 2024. According to the indictment, the same network recruited a U.S. citizen in Lithuania to surveil another Kremlin critic before allegedly offering about $25,000 to kill him. After that recruit refused, prosecutors say the network shifted to soliciting sabotage attacks against infrastructure in countries supporting Ukraine, including alleged plots targeting electrical substations , warehouses and transportation hubs. The indictment comes as Western governments have warned that Russia has expanded its use of covert operations, sabotage and assassination plots beyond the battlefield since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. articles.title: Ex-Dem insider drops bombshell on where Harris ranked in secret poll for Biden replacements
articles.summary: Lindy Li says Democratic internal polling showed Kamala Harris ranked dead last among potential Biden replacements, behind Pete Buttigieg and others.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, says Democrats had internal polling showing that Kamala Harris was far from the party’s best shot at beating Donald Trump. But that polling wasn’t convenient. "The polling numbers went directly against the narrative that the party wanted to espouse," Li said. "They knew that skipping over Kamala Harris would be a slap in the face to the bedrock of the party, which is Black women in particular, and they just wouldn't have it," Li told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. EX-DEM INSIDER EXPOSES WHAT HARRIS TOLD TOP DONORS DAYS BEFORE BIDEN DROPPED OUT: 'INSULTING' Li is chronicling the months leading up to Biden's withdrawal from the race in her new book, "Unburdened," revealing that the party’s internal thinking behind why Harris was made the nominee and how many of the party’s top figures had long known that Biden’s age had created an unavoidable political liability. Li recalled that former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Harris had been floated as possible replacements for Biden before Biden announced his decision to step down. According to Li, Harris was at the bottom of the group. "Kamala Harris came in dead last. It wasn't even close. Pete Buttigieg, who hilariously received 0% support from the Black vote, did better than she did. And yet the party is so straitjacketed by DEI that they had no choice but to appoint her," Li said. As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). She recalled how the polling was guarded closely, but that it circulated among the party’s leading operatives and fundraisers like herself. FORMER DNC FUNDRAISER SAYS MAJOR DONORS WON’T BACK KAMALA HARRIS AGAIN AS PARTY FACES DIVISIONS "I’m part of the National Finance Committee. The list of membership is guarded like the papal conclave. But people talk. It's a very small group of people. That poll was commissioned internally," Li said. "Most of the time I would say I don't believe a candidate's polling because it's basically just funded propaganda. But in this case, we wanted an objective overview of who could actually mount the most formidable opposition to Trump." At the end of the day, Li believes that the decision to put Harris at the top of the ticket was made, at least partially, out of fear. In addition to being the vice president and an obvious replacement consideration for Biden, Li recalled that Harris had devoted followers who would make it painful to explore other options. "People were terrified of the online mob. The K-Hive isn’t that numerous, but they’re very, very toxic and they’re very coordinated. No one wants to be labeled as a racist," Li said, referring to the nickname for Harris’ supporters. Li believes that, using that fear and by positioning herself close to Biden’s donors, Harris made herself the choice the party couldn’t turn a blind eye to, despite knowledge of her weakness as a candidate. HOW TRUMP PANIC BROKE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY AND FUELED ENDLESS CRISIS POLITICS "Oscar-worthy. Honestly, truly Oscar-worthy," Li said. articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: House control could hinge on whether the old political rules still apply
articles.summary: Trump's mid-30s approval and high gas prices favor Democrats, but redistricting and turnout questions could keep House races razor-tight.
articles.body: Are we playing with the old playbook or a new playbook in the midterm elections this fall? That’s unclear. It’s hard to determine simply because we’ve seen so much that’s "new" in politics lately. Norms are cast aside. The American system quaked to its core in recent years. You’ve witnessed an American president win the election by prevailing in the Electoral College but losing the popular vote. To have that happen twice in 16 years (2000 and 2016) is astonishing, considering the fact that such an outcome only unfolded on three occasions before. You then had a president impeached twice yet return to office a few years later. There was the Capitol riot as arguing continued about the 2020 election. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT If this is the old playbook, Democrats likely light up the scoreboard in November. The party of the president typically loses about 25 seats in a president’s first midterm. Midterm elections are frequently a referendum on the president. That’s why many Republicans are trying to keep President Donald Trump at arm’s length, considering that his polling numbers are anywhere from the mid-30s to 40% on a good day. Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are skyrocketing. The war in Iran lingers. There’s a trade war with one of America’s best allies. On the old playbook, this portends a disaster for the GOP in this fall’s midterms. But what if we’re using the new playbook? President Trump — and sometimes Republicans aligned with him — have shown a remarkable resilience to defy political gravity and norms. Control of the House could come down to just a few seats. What if there are questions about election security and the validity of who won and lost? There’s redistricting. On paper, Republicans probably redrew about five to six seats nationwide in their favor. If things are tight, we might not know which party wins the House on election night. Perhaps a few days down the road — if not later. That is, unless it’s a Democratic blowout. And remember what we said a few moments ago about the president’s party losing so many seats in that first midterm? Yes, in a way, this is President Trump’s "first midterm." But not really. He experienced a midterm in 2018. Not that things went in the GOP’s favor that year. There’s no contemporary data on how the party of a president might perform after he’s been out of office and rallied to victory a few years later. Also, the sheer reduction by both parties of seats which are in play mitigates political "waves" which crash across the political shoreline in House midterm races. Think 1994 and 2010 for Republicans. 2018 for Democrats. Thus, even though many of the factors favor the Democrats, the possibility remains it could be tough for the party to flip the House. In 2018, the Democrats’ carried an approval rating of 44%. For this time around, it’s 37%. That rivals polling related to the president. In 2018, voters had had enough of President Trump and wanted a change. But because of the polling parity this year, it’s not so obvious that voters are so turned off by President Trump that they automatically gravitate to the Democrats. Here’s another factor: turnout. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY? President Trump has worked hard to tell voters that he’s "on the ballot" this fall. That cuts two ways. President Trump’s presence on the ballot has historically driven people to the polls. In 2016, 60.1% of registered voters showed up. In 2020, an eye-popping 66.4% of all voters cast ballots. And in 2024, 64.3% of those registered to vote did so. But considering the president’s unpopularity, the cognizance of voters that he’s "on the ballot" could also deter them from turning out. At least those who previously supported him. And those impacts ricochet down to House races. The president’s track record at turning out independent voters in races that count wasn’t great down ballot even as he won the White House in 2024. Consider that, in the 2018 midterms, 50.1% of registered voters materialized. Just 46.1% voted in the 2022 midterms. It was 36.1% in the 2014 midterms — 41% in the historic 2010 midterms where Republicans won a record 63 House seats. This "Trump on the ballot" initiative might not resound with voters. Especially since the president conceded — en route to his midterm convention in Dallas — that gas prices wouldn’t decrease until after the election. He also said the U.S. is stuck with the war in Iran through the midterms. So, how do we know what to anticipate in November? It’s really hard to read if there’s not a clear wave coming. The best way to postulate control of the House is by going race to race. And that is a painstaking process. For instance, will Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., have a district in which to run? Missouri Republicans tried to draw Cleaver out of his district earlier this year. Then a court ruled last week that the Show-Me State must use the old congressional districts, likely meaning that Cleaver was safe. Then another judge ruled that voters already cast ballots in primaries. So, the new maps were back, and Cleaver may be out. All of this less than two months before the election. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING Is there a groundswell for Democrats in Iowa where the Senate seat and governor’s mansion are in jeopardy for Republicans? If that’s the case, Democrats might have a shot of claiming at least two if not three seats there: Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and maybe the seat that Rep. Ashley Hinson is vacating in her quest to become a senator. How about Ohio? There are competitive gubernatorial and Senate contests. Does a Democratic surge boost Rep. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio? Do the accusations of spousal and child abuse bounce embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio., in what is otherwise a relatively safe Republican seat? Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, clung to her seat by fewer than 1,000 votes two years ago. But that was when President Trump carried the Buckeye State by 11 points and Kaptur’s district. Redistricting actually turned Kaptur’s turf slightly more in her favor. But the 80-year-old Kaptur was in a car wreck in August, inhibiting her ability to campaign. Is that a factor? How well do Democrats perform in Virginia? Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, D-Va., who she vanquished in 2022. Could former Rep. Tom Perriello, D-Va., who won in a 2008 upset in a differently-drawn district and promptly lost in 2010, unseat Rep. John McGuire, R-Va.? Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, is retiring. Former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage is running for Golden’s seat. Does LePage benefit from Democratic chaos in the effort to unseat Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine? After all, President Trump won one of Maine’s three electoral votes in 2024, capturing that congressional district over former Vice President Kamala Harris. We could bounce around the map, district to district, all day like this. But sans a wave, that’s what you must do to properly filet the House races. Most conventional arrows point in the direction of Democrats winning the House this fall. Yet it probably shouldn’t be this close. That’s why you have to go by the playbook. articles.title: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles says she’s cancer-free
articles.summary: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles announced Wednesday that she is now cancer-free after being diagnosed with breast cancer in March.
articles.body: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles announced Wednesday that she is now cancer-free after being diagnosed with breast cancer in March. “After a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, my pathology results came back clear. I am cancer free,” she wrote in a post on X. Wiles, 69, who has served as President Donald Trump’s White House chief of staff since the beginning of his second term, thanked him for his “unwavering support.” She added that she’s “deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda.” She first announced in mid-March that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, which had been caught in the early stages, and that she’d received a “strong prognosis.” According to the American Cancer Society, breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed among women in the U.S. and is the second-leading cause of death from cancer among women, with lung cancer being first. It’s not clear what type of breast cancer Wiles had. Trump had first disclosed Wiles’ diagnosis on Truth Social before she released an update about her health, saying that she would receive treatment. At the time, the president added that Wiles would be “spending virtually full time at the White House, which makes me, as President, very happy!” He added, “Her Strength and her Commitment to continue doing the job she loves, and does so well, while undergoing treatment, tells you everything you need to know about her. Susie, as one of my closest and most important advisors, is tough and deeply committed to serving the American People. She will soon be better than ever!”

articles.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
articles.summary: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.
articles.body:
The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.

Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".

After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."

In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.

The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.

In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".

"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.

The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.

Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.

The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons.

The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

articles.title: Top Democrat puts hold on Trump’s $2.8B weapons sale to Israel
articles.summary: The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the rare step Wednesday of publicly announcing a hold on the Trump administration’s $2.8 billion plan to sell 40,000 one-ton bombs to Israel. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the panel, said in a statement posted to X that he remains firmly committed…
articles.body:
The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the rare step Wednesday of publicly announcing a hold on the Trump administration’s $2.8 billion plan to sell 40,000 one-ton bombs to Israel.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the panel, said in a statement posted to X that he remains firmly committed to Israel’s security and its ability to defend itself, but raised concern about the risk to civilian lives, given the high death tolls throughout Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza, and against Hezbollah in Lebanon.

“I therefore will not clear this sale at this time. The decision does not diminish Congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs; it reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that U.S.-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly, and with meaningful safeguards for human life.”

Meeks’ decision to publicize his opposition, which generally takes place behind the scenes and with an effort toward compromise, represents Democrats’ frustration with the Trump administration and toward the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The top lawmakers on the House and Senate foreign affairs panels are generally informed by the State Department about a foreign arms sale over a certain dollar amount, and are given the opportunity to exercise an informal “hold” for more information on the arms sale before it goes forward.

The State Department typically respects this hold and works with the member to resolve their concerns. But the Trump administration has previously ignored an objection from Meeks, moving forward on an arms sale package in February 2025 despite the Democrats “hold” on parts of the sale.

The Hill reached out to the State Department for comment.

The weapons package, reported by the Washington Post, includes 40,000 bombs that weigh 2,000 pounds each. These include 20,000 MK-84s and 20,000 BLU-117s. The sale also includes 20,000 I2000 Penetrator warheads, the Post reported.

The MK-84, in particular, is capable of forming a crater 50 feet wide and 36 ft deep and can penetrate up to 15 inches of metal or 11 ft of concrete, and projects “legal fragmentation” to a radius of 400 yards, according to army data.

During Israel’s war in Gaza, the Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000 pound bombs out of concern for the rising death toll of Palestinian civilians. The New York Times reported in 2023 that Israel’s use of the 2,000 pound bombs posed a pervasive threat to Gaza civilians seeking safety, with the munitions routinely dropped in areas designated for civilians.

While there’s still bipartisan backing of the U.S. and Israel relationship in Congress, that support is waning, in particular among Democrats. When Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) forced a vote on bill text to cut off U.S. military aid to Israel, it received support from 103 Democrats.

articles.title: Republican US senator slams Trump vaccine policy amid rising measles deaths
articles.summary: US Senator Bill Cassidy presses Trump’s pick for surgeon general on views over vaccines, public health.
articles.body:
Republican Senator Bill Cassidy has blamed the Trump administration’s vaccination policies for an uptick in measles deaths in the United States, where the preventable disease had previously been all but eliminated.

Cassidy , a doctor who chairs the Senate Health Committee and represents the US state of Louisiana, said on Wednesday that the government must appoint officials to key public health positions who will make decisions based on science rather than political ideology.

“To suffer from any disease is awful, but to suffer one which is avoidable, that’s even worse,” Cassidy said.

The US is currently facing its most severe measles outbreak in more than 35 years, a development that scientists and public health experts attribute to increasing scepticism towards vaccinations that have helped largely eliminate diseases such as measles.

Cassidy stated that three people have died from a measles outbreak in the state of Pennsylvania , with a fourth death still under review.

Members of the Trump administration, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. and the president himself, have been criticised for promoting debunked claims linking vaccines to autism.

The Republican senator pressed Dr Nicole Saphier, the Trump administration’s nominee for surgeon general, for a straightforward answer on whether she believes the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine causes autism.

Saphier initially stated that she has “not seen reputable evidence” that vaccines cause autism. Under further questioning from Cassidy, who called her answer a “bit of an equivocation”, she said that the MMR vaccine was “our greatest tool for combating measles” and that she did not believe that childhood vaccines cause autism.

The health committee is currently weighing Trump’s nominations of Saphier for surgeon general, along with Chris Klomp for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services and Dr Timothy Westlake to lead the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. All of whom need Senate confirmation for their roles

The US has not had a surgeon general since January 2025, as Trump’s two previous picks have faced opposition and questions in the Senate about their qualifications. Saphier is a radiologist and former Fox News contributor.

Cassidy, who lost his Republican primary election in May after attracting Trump’s ire over his vote to impeach the president in 2021, has become an outspoken Republican critic of the government’s approach to vaccines and public health.

articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Anxieties over data centers have cranked up considerably, and one Senate Republican wants to close a tax loophole that he argues tech giants are using as "corporate welfare" to build facilities throughout the country. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., plans on introducing legislation that would tie up a tax loophole for data centers first unleashed by Republicans in 2017 that he charged has been exploited by tech companies to build their sprawling data center facilities. It comes as the GOP wrestles with how to handle the data center and AI issue, which has become a major political wedge on the campaign trail, one President Donald Trump has called a "hoax." 'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN That loophole, Hawley told Fox News Digital in an interview, is for Opportunity Zones, which he said are generally meant for "for low-income areas, low-income housing, low-income businesses or businesses in low-income areas." "These data centers have figured out a way that they think that they can access all of this money," Hawley said. "So, let's be clear. This is a form of corporate welfare. They don't need any welfare. These people are rich. They can pay their own way." The tax breaks were first approved by Congress as part of Trump’s first-term tax cuts package, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. That initial bite at the apple established them as a means to spur investment into lower income or forgotten areas where tracts of land were dubbed Opportunity Zones. AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE They were then made permanent last year through the "big, beautiful bill," and though not explicitly intended to be used for data centers, have since provided a route for tech companies to defer, reduce or outright eliminate corporate gains taxes on their investments in the zones. Since both tax packages were passed, 8,746 Opportunity Zones have cropped up in the U.S., according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, just under half of all zones are in rural areas, where tech goliaths have set their sights on building data centers. And, according to a report from the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, 14% of all data centers are in Opportunity Zones, while just over 17% of all permitted, approved and under construction data center projects are in the zones. Hawley's forthcoming bill would explicitly exclude data centers from being able to access the tax cuts, adding another barrier at the federal level in an attempt to try and slow their rapid development. And it comes as Congress scrambles to answer the growing fears over unfettered AI development, which data centers play a key role in. articles.title: House moves to hold Leon Black in contempt of Congress over Epstein interview
articles.summary: The House swiftly approved a motion to hold billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he failed to appear for a deposition on his ties to late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, passing the referral to the Justice Department through unanimous consent. The House Oversight Committee unanimously agreed to hold Black in contempt…
articles.body:
The House swiftly approved a motion to hold billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he failed to appear for a deposition on his ties to late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, passing the referral to the Justice Department through unanimous consent.

The House Oversight Committee unanimously agreed to hold Black in contempt of Congress on Tuesday night, and Chair James Comer’s (R-Ky.) move to forward the measure through unanimous consent on the House floor Wednesday was not objected to, though the matter did not receive a formal vote before all members.

“No one is above the law. Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the U.S. House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors in our investigation of the federal government’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases,” Comer said in a statement after the measure passed.

Lawmakers have sought to question Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management, about payments he made to Epstein — totaling millions over a number of years. The investor says he had no knowledge of the late financier’s abuse, asserting the payments only went toward business matters like tax and estate planning .

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the panel, saw contempt as a step to gaining insight into the financial entanglements between the two men.

“This vote is an important step towards justice and accountability. Leon Black has continued to defy two congressional subpoenas and we need to know why he gave Jeffrey Epstein $180 million dollars. We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes. We are just getting started,” Garcia said.

A contempt resolution acts as a referral to the Justice Department, which determines whether or not to bring charges.

Black walked out of a voluntary interview with the panel about the Epstein investigation two months ago, and he sued the committee earlier this month on the day he was commanded to appear for a deposition.

His lawsuit argues the committee lacks legal authority to enforce the subpoenas and that they improperly seek private information.

“Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the complaint states.

Black’s attorneys on Wednesday accused Comer and the committee of rushing ahead to recommend charges.

“This an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black. The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry,” attorneys Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler said in a statement.

They continued, “First, the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chairman Comer rushed to issue him subpoenas. Then, the Committee rushed to hold him in contempt, even in the face of active litigation and an ethics complaint. Now, the full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee’s actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer.”

“Mr. Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein’s victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein. He never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein. Mr. Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct.”

articles.title: El-Sayed visits Senate Democrats, who are starting to warm to him
articles.summary: Senate Democrats are starting to warm to Michigan Senate Abdul El-Sayed after a Wednesday meeting at their campaign arm’s headquarters, though muted reactions from some lawmakers indicated the progressive Senate nominee has work to do with the caucus ahead of November. “He’s a great candidate,” said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), chair of the Senate Democrats’…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats are starting to warm to Michigan Senate Abdul El-Sayed after a Wednesday meeting at their campaign arm’s headquarters, though muted reactions from some lawmakers indicated the progressive Senate nominee has work to do with the caucus ahead of November.

“He’s a great candidate,” said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), chair of the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm. “We haven’t lost Michigan in 30 years. He’s energizing the base, and I’m very optimistic.”

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) told reporters he was “all in” for El-Sayed, who said he was “opening up a structural lead.”

“They have tried to paint him as something when he comes across so accessible to a lot of voters, and we’re starting to see that in the data, which means he’s connecting [with] Michiganders,” Heinrich said. “And at the end of the day, I think the things that are really driving this election cycle are the out-of-control costs of everything from groceries to gasoline.”

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) told reporters he planned to campaign with El-Sayed ahead of November, while Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) indicated he would be open to hitting the stump for the progressive former Wayne County health director if he was asked.

Both Kelly and Murphy are seen as potential 2028 presidential contenders.

“Abdul is going to be able to cross over and get conservative, traditionally Republican support in Michigan, and I think he’ll be more of a bridge builder here than folks think he will be,” Murphy said.

As he headed to his meeting with Senate Democrats, El-Sayed told reporters that “we’re having really productive conversations about what it takes to win,” when asked if he had reached out to Senate Democratic leadership about spending in the race.

El-Sayed said he was “looking forward to a productive meeting” with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who backed Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) over El-Sayed in the primary. El-Sayed added that “all pathways to a Senate majority run through Michigan.”

Other Democrats offered more muted responses when asked about their party’s meeting with the Michigan Senate candidate, whose position over Israel and progressive stances on issues have rankled some members.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), another potential White House hopeful in 2028, did not answer questions about how the meeting went with El-Sayed. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) also offered little on the meeting, calling it “peachy” and “just a private conversation.”

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), who rushed in and out of the meeting, told reporters the progressive was “great” and suggested he would be a “fabulous” member.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) offered little details about the meeting, too, but said that he looked “forward to welcoming him to our team in January.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), a supporter of the Michigan Senate candidate, described the meeting as “informal” with “lots of hugs and lots of just this and that.”

Schumer was expected to meet with El-Sayed later on Wednesday.

El-Sayed, a critic of Israel, has frustrated some Democrats by describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide” and being opposed to offering unconditional aid to Israel.

His closeness to far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who’s made controversial remarks in the past including that “America deserved 9/11,” has also roiled El-Sayed’s bid as both Democrats and Republicans have pressed the progressive to denounce his ally. El-Sayed has said he doesn’t have any plans to campaign with Piker before November.

El-Sayed has sought to make inroads with Jewish voters, including by apologizing for saying “hurt people hurt people” in response to an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this spring, which the FBI characterized as “a Hizballah-inspired act of terrorism.”

A group of Jewish Democrats, including former Sen. Al Franken (D-Minn.) and former Rep. Andy Levin (D-Mich.) also signed their name on a letter expressing their support for El-Sayed, according to a copy of the letter first obtained by The Washington Post.

“Although most Jewish Americans can easily support Dr. El-Sayed’s domestic agenda, his foreign policy positions and statements on Israel and Iran have been a concern for many,” the letter said. “But his positions are much less outside the mainstream of the contemporary foreign-policy debate than some of the charged rhetoric surrounding his candidacy might suggest.”

Meanwhile, a group of Jewish leaders and rabbis in Michigan offered their own petition , which pressed El-Sayed to change some of his stances around the issue without directly naming him.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Michigan Senate race a “toss up.”

articles.title: Americans warned to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on Wednesday warned Americans to reconsider traveling to Saudi Arabia amid the threat of Iranian drone and missile strikes targeting U.S. assets in the country. Embassy officials shared this in a Level 3 travel advisory that also warned of threats of “armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans, and local laws regarding social…
articles.body:
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on Wednesday warned Americans to reconsider traveling to Saudi Arabia amid the threat of Iranian drone and missile strikes targeting U.S. assets in the country.

Embassy officials shared this in a Level 3 travel advisory that also warned of threats of “armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans, and local laws regarding social media activity,” with some areas facing an increased risk. They urged that no one travel to the border with Yemen due to terror threats.

“Terrorism is a concern in Saudi Arabia,” the advisory reads. “Attacks can occur with little or no warning, especially around holidays. They can involve knives, firearms, and vehicles. Terrorists may use violence to respond to direct attacks against them or other military operations in the region.”

Along with the threat from Iran, the embassy said the regime’s proxy in Yemen, the Houthis, has renewed threats to attack Saudi Arabia.

Officials advised that U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia are not allowed to travel within 20 miles of the border with Yemen or to the Persian Gulf city of Al Qatif “for non-essential travel due to safety risks.”

These risks extend to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran and Qatif, though employees must have special authorization to travel to these regions.

Last Friday, the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia’s 745-mile-long East-West Pipeline, a vital pipeline that has moved crude production from the Persian Gulf ports to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, where tankers can export oil.

Saudi officials shut down the pipeline, which could take 3-5 weeks to prepare. The pipeline moved a weekly average of 2.6 million to 4 million barrels a day since late August.

Oil prices jumped 4 percent on Monday and have remained steady two days later. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent crude , settled at $105.49 per barrel as of Wednesday afternoon. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , the benchmark in the U.S., rose to $102.05. AAA estimated that the national average for gas in the U.S. is $4.37.

The price hikes have also followed Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported.

President Trump has not spoken out about this attack or other attacks on key energy pipelines and reportedly rebuffed a request from Saudi Arabia to launch strikes on the Houthis. The U.S. has sent advisers to support the kingdom.

Trump previously authorized strikes on the Houthis in March 2025 after the rebels attacks commercial vessels in the Red Sea. He warned in July that he would “ hold Iran responsible ” if the Houthis launch more attacks on ships in the Red Sea after two Saudi oil tankers were attacked.

articles.body:
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles said that she is “cancer free” on Wednesday after announcing earlier this year she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer.

Wiles wrote in a post on X that her pathology results came back clear after a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.

“Thank you to my family, friends, doctors, and everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way,” she wrote.

“A special thank you to President Trump for his unwavering support. I am deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda,” she continued.

Wiles announced earlier this year that she had been diagnosed with early stage breast cancer.

“She’s an amazing person, an amazing fighter, and she announced a minor difficulty which will be in good shape. You’ll be around for a long time,” Trump told reporters while sitting next Wiles in March. “She’s going to be in great shape. The prognosis is excellent.”

Wiles is considered one of Trump’s closest advisers and has played an integral role in shaping his second administration. Wiles also was instrumental in Trump’s election win in 2024.

While the chief of staff is often seen at Trump’s side, Wiles is known for keeping a low profile.

articles.body:
The Senate Agriculture Committee passed “Farm Bill 2.0” out of committee on Wednesday following Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R- Ky.) return to Congress.

The vote passed 12-11 along party lines. Despite Democratic opposition, the bill was able to move forward once McConnell returned to the panel this week.

The senator was previously absent from Congress following a serious fall at his Washington home in June. During his absence, the panel was unable to pass the farm bill as Democrats voted together to block the legislation.

The farm bill is a sprawling agriculture and food aid package normally passed every five years. Congress has not passed a farm bill since 2018. The House passed its latest version in April.

Democrats on the panel have pushed back against a provision in the bill that would require states to help cover the cost of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) funding alongside the federal government if payment error rates in a state exceeded a certain point.

Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), the panel’s chair, compromised with Democrats, who had expressed concern about the provision earlier this summer, by offering a one-year delay.

“The rest of the story is this: we offered a one-year delay with no payment, no cost. It was rejected,” Boozman said during Wednesday’s meeting. “We’re running out of time, and we’re rapidly losing a window that we can actually get this thing passed.”

Boozman defended the provision, stating the intention behind it was to give states “the help they needed, get them under control, where they didn’t have error rates of 20-25 percent.”

The panel’s Democrats said the delay was not enough time for states like Minnesota and Colorado.

“We share this goal of reducing error rates, but we recognize the reality that states across the country need time and equal resources to bring them down,” Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), the ranking member on the panel, said during the meeting. “I appreciate Chairman Bozeman’s offer in this bill and the inclusion in this bill of this one-year delay, and it is a big start from where we were.”

The meeting started with an attempted amendment by Sen. Joni Ernest (R-Iowa) about the Save Our Bacon Act, but Boozman closed the door on her, saying, “you had the opportunity.”

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) also attempted to make another amendment about stockyards and packers but was similarly shut down by the chair.
